abstract: This paper addresses the question of whether and how artificial intelligence systems can be considered agents, framing it as a 'demarcation problem' in social theory. Rather than treating agency as an inherent property of a system, the authors argue that agency is a social status—a socially granted and monitored license to issue actions. They develop theoretical criteria to distinguish agents from nonagents based on the abilities socially attributed to entities.
key_claims: Agency is not an inherent quality of a system but a socially granted status or license to act.
This social license is acquired and monitored through social practices.
The demarcation between agents and nonagents can be theoretically grounded in socially attributed abilities.
Recent AI developments make the question of machine agency urgent for social theory.
methods: Conceptual and theoretical analysis grounded in social theory.
Development of demarcation criteria to distinguish agents from nonagents.
Reframing of agency as an attributed social status rather than an intrinsic system property.
findings: A framework (described by the authors as a 'matrix of AI agency') can be used to classify entities according to the abilities socially attributed to them.
Machine agency is contingent on social recognition and ongoing monitoring within social practices rather than on technical capability alone.
contributions: Offers a social-theoretic account of AI agency that shifts the debate from system properties to social attribution.
Proposes theoretical criteria for demarcating agents and nonagents.
Introduces a conceptual matrix for situating AI within questions of agency.
framing: The paper situates itself within social theory and the sociology of agency, engaging debates over machine agency prompted by advances in AI. It positions its social-status conception of agency against views that treat agency as an inherent quality of a system.
